```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = FALSE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Use `oauth_db_postgres()` to query your own PostgreSQL server with the
visitor's OAuth access token. PostgreSQL validates the token and maps its
identity to a database role; normal grants and row-level security determine
which data the visitor can read.

## Try the Docker playground

Check out `lukakoning/shinyOAuth` and `lukakoning/shinyOAuthDB` into sibling
directories, then start Docker with Linux containers. From the shinyOAuthDB
repository root, run:

```r
source("playground/postgres/run.R")
```

Docker supplies R, Shiny, PostgreSQL 18, Keycloak, a token validator and a
local certificate authority. The first image build compiles PostgreSQL and
installs the R dependencies. Open `http://localhost:18100` once Shiny starts;
your browser may ask you to trust the local test certificate at
`https://localhost:18443`.

Sign in as `alice` with `alice-fixture-password`, or `bob` with
`bob-fixture-password`. Each account sees two rows belonging to that role,
although the app runs the same SQL for both. PostgreSQL applies the row
policy. The controls also let you refresh the token, check table grants,
attempt the other role, and sign out. Click **Stop playground** to remove
its containers and test data. If you force the launcher to exit, use the
cleanup command it printed at startup.

All accounts and credentials in this fixture are public test data. PostgreSQL
stays inside Docker; the browser ports bind only to the host's loopback
interface. Use your own credentials, certificates and hostnames in a deployment.

## Native runtime

The current native adapter supports Linux with libpq major version 18.
Both RPostgres and shinyOAuthDB must link the same shared libpq instance.
Build libpq with `--without-libcurl` and leave the optional `libpq-oauth`
device-flow module uninstalled. shinyOAuth obtains tokens through browser
sign-in; a retained broken database handle must not start another login.

For a custom Linux image, install libpq's development files and `pkg-config`,
point `PKG_CONFIG_PATH` and the dynamic library search path at that libpq,
then build RPostgres and shinyOAuthDB from source:

```r
install.packages("RPostgres", type = "source")
Sys.setenv(SHINYOAUTHDB_POSTGRES_OAUTH = "required")
install.packages(".", repos = NULL, type = "source")
```

Run the last command from the shinyOAuthDB checkout, or replace `"."` with
the path to its source directory or source tarball. Setting `SHINYOAUTHDB_POSTGRES_OAUTH` to
`required` makes installation fail if the native adapter cannot be built.
The default, `auto`, builds it when the required Linux/libpq 18 development
files are available. `disabled` builds the other backends without this adapter.
Windows and macOS can use the Linux Docker playground.

## Configure PostgreSQL and Keycloak

PostgreSQL's native OAuth needs an installed token-validation module. The
example uses Percona's `pg_oidc_validator`, pinned and patched to validate
the database audience. See `integration/postgres-keycloak/Dockerfile` and
`patches/validator-audience.patch` in the checkout for the exact build.

Register a Web OAuth client in Keycloak with your Shiny callback URL,
authorization code flow and PKCE. Configure the database access token's
audience and the `database.read` scope. The fixture's
`realm-shinyoauthdb.json` provides a complete example, including fixed test
subjects and clients with deliberately incorrect audiences or missing scopes.

Configure PostgreSQL's validator to check token signatures, issuer, expiry,
audience and the required scope. Map the validated subject to a database
role. A corresponding `pg_hba.conf` rule looks like:

```text
hostssl reporting alice,bob 10.0.0.0/24 oauth issuer="https://login.example.org/realms/reporting" scope="database.read" validator=pg_oidc_validator map=keycloak_subjects
```

In `pg_ident.conf`, map the real Keycloak subjects to roles:

```text
keycloak_subjects 11111111-1111-4111-8111-111111111111 alice
keycloak_subjects 22222222-2222-4222-8222-222222222222 bob
```

Those subjects are examples from the local fixture; use your provider's real
values. Create the roles, grant database access, and configure table grants
and row policies. The checkout includes complete files under
`integration/postgres-keycloak/config/` and SQL under `sql/01-fixture.sql`.

## Shiny app

Create a shinyOAuth client for your own issuer. Request `profile` and
configure the provider to include `preferred_username` in the validated ID
token. This example assumes that username matches the PostgreSQL role
provisioned for that person, as in the Docker fixture. Set
`OAUTHDB_POSTGRES_ISSUER`, `OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID`, and `OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET`
before running the app.

```{r app, eval=FALSE}
library(shiny)
library(shinyOAuth)
library(shinyOAuthDB)

issuer <- Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_POSTGRES_ISSUER")
provider <- oauth_provider_oidc_discover(issuer, id_token_validation = TRUE)
client <- oauth_client(
  provider,
  client_id = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID"),
  client_secret = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET"),
  redirect_uri = "http://localhost:8100",
  scopes = c("openid", "profile", "database.read")
)

ui <- oauth_ui(fluidPage(
  actionButton("login", "Sign in"),
  actionButton("logout", "Sign out"),
  tableOutput("rows")
), id = "auth", client = client)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  auth <- oauth_module_server("auth", client, auto_redirect = FALSE)
  observeEvent(input$login, auth$request_login())
  observeEvent(input$logout, auth$logout())

  con <- oauth_db_postgres(
    auth$connection,
    host = "postgres.example.org", dbname = "reporting",
    user = function() {
      reference <- req(auth$connection())
      identity <- reference$identity(claims = "preferred_username")
      req(identity$id_token_claims$preferred_username)
    },
    issuer = issuer, scope = "database.read",
    sslrootcert = "path/to/ca.pem"
  )
  output$rows <- renderTable({
    connection <- con()
    DBI::dbGetQuery(connection, "SELECT current_user AS database_user")
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server, options = list(port = 8100), uiPattern = ".*")
```

`user` is the database role requested when opening a PostgreSQL
connection. The callback derives it from the currently signed-in account's
validated identity, so signing in as a different person changes the
requested role. PostgreSQL checks that the access token is allowed to use
that role and applies its grants and row policies.

If your database roles differ from the provider's usernames, adapt the
callback to your server's identity-to-role mapping. The subjects mapped
to `alice` and `bob` above are Docker fixture configuration, not a list of
visitors to hardcode into a deployed app. A fixed `user` is appropriate only
when the deployment intentionally maps the permitted identities to one
shared database role.

The checkout's `playground/example-postgres.R` uses the same dynamic
identity selection with connection settings from environment variables.

## Connection lifetime and tests

Call `con()` before every operation. Ordinary token refresh preserves a
valid database connection. Sign-out, permission loss, an account change or
the end of the Shiny session closes it. A failed connection can be replaced
through `con()` with a current token; resetting or cloning an old native
connection is unsupported. Keep separate workers in separate R processes.

The PostgreSQL OAuth GitHub Actions workflow runs independently of the usual
package checks. It installs the current package and the shinyOAuth checkout
inside the pinned Docker environment, then runs native cleanup checks and
real browser tests. The suite requires zero failures, warnings or skips.

See the [PostgreSQL OAuth documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/auth-oauth.html)
and [libpq's bearer-token hook](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/libpq-oauth.html)
for the underlying interfaces. Azure's Entra authentication uses a separate
[Azure PostgreSQL helper](azure-postgres.html).
